metadata.note: The Grand Trunk Railway's original main line (built as the Atlantic and St. Lawrence Railroad on the US side, joined at the border by the St. Lawrence and Atlantic Railroad on the Canadian side, both absorbed into Grand Trunk in 1853, later Canadian National): Montreal to Portland, Maine, via the Eastern Townships of Quebec, Island Pond VT, Berlin NH, Bethel ME and Lewiston ME. This was the reason the line existed at all -- Portland businessman John A. Poor lobbied to make Portland (ice-free year-round, unlike the St. Lawrence) Montreal's winter Atlantic port, about 100 miles closer than Boston. It made Lewiston a stop on an international main line, not just a branch. Regular Montreal-Portland operations began April 4 1853, with the final construction link completed that July, making it North America's first international railroad. Grand Trunk was nationalized into Canadian National Railways in 1923. Passenger service survived in shrinking form afterward -- a daily Montreal-Portland/Lewiston train as of a 1954 timetable, reduced to a weekly, summer-only Sunday train by the mid-1960s, discontinued in 1967. Geometry is real-traced from OpenStreetMap over the surviving right-of-way, which the St. Lawrence and Atlantic short line still occupies end to end; only the last 1.08 miles into the Portland terminal are approximated. Tracing the real alignment also corrected the route: the main line does not pass through Lewiston. It runs Mechanic Falls - Lewiston Junction - Danville Junction - Yarmouth, 5.6 miles west of Lewiston, and the city was served by a 5.4-mile branch off Lewiston Junction, drawn here as a separate feature. The earlier straight-line geometry ran the main line through Lewiston itself and skipped Danville Junction entirely. Richmond, QC was itself a key junction where this line met the separate Grand Trunk branch to Quebec City.

metadata.geometry_audit: 2026-08-26: geometry replaced. Both main-line features had carried the same 19-point straight-line waypoint chain (271.7 mi, one point every 15 mi); they now carry a 929-point OpenStreetMap trace (294.00 mi) checked against the published milepost list. The retrace moved the main line off Lewiston and onto Danville Junction, its real alignment, and the Lewiston branch was added as two new features so the city is not lost from the map. See CLAUDE.md Rule 2.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap over the surviving right-of-way, 929 points, Montreal to Portland MP 1.5. Traced length 292.92 mi; total drawn 294.00 mi. ONE APPROXIMATED LEG: the final 1.08 mi, from the last mapped point of the ex-Grand Trunk line in East Deering (MP ~1.5) to the Grand Trunk terminal at India and Commercial Streets (MP 0), is a single straight line. Nothing survives there to trace -- the Back Cove Trestle burned in 1984 and the waterfront terminal trackage is gone -- so that mile and a half is a chord across Back Cove, not a surveyed alignment. Everything north of it is real track. Checked against the documented mileposts on the US half: Yarmouth 11.26 vs 11.3, Danville Junction 26.96 vs 27.6, Mechanic Falls 35.92 vs 36.2, Oxford 40.79 vs 40.9, South Paris 47.45 vs 47.3, Bethel 69.34 vs 70.1, Gorham 91.23 vs 91.6, Berlin 97.43 vs 97.9, Island Pond 149.08 vs 149.5 -- every one within 0.8 mi over 149 miles (0.997x at Island Pond). The Quebec half has no published milepost list here; its stations sit on the trace in the documented order (Saint-Lambert, Saint-Hyacinthe, Sainte-Rosalie, Acton Vale, Richmond, Windsor, Bromptonville, Sherbrooke, Lennoxville, Coaticook, Norton), each within 0.43 mi of it. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 1 ruled segment totalling 15 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

segments.note: The Grand Trunk opened this 5.4-mile branch from Lewiston Junction (MP 29.7 on the Montreal-Portland main line) into Lewiston in 1874, and built the depot that still stands there the same year. It is why the station list for this route names Lewiston: the main line itself passes 5.6 miles west of the city through Danville Junction, and Lewiston was reached by a section off the main train, not by trains running through the city. Frequency estimated/unsourced
sources: Segment-level (route and length only): the branch, its 1874 opening and its 5.4-mile length come from the milepost list for Lewiston Junction MP 29.7. The end year is NOT sourced at segment level -- see the note.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, 34 points: the city-owned Lewiston and Auburn Railroad (the surviving ex-Grand Trunk stub) from Lewiston Junction, then the abandoned alignment beyond it. Traced 5.42 mi against the documented 5.4-mile branch -- a 1.00x match. The trace stops 0.49 mi short of the Grand Trunk depot on Lincoln Street: that last half mile through downtown Lewiston is lifted and unmapped, and is NOT drawn rather than approximated. Maine Central trackage in Lewiston (the CSX Waterville Subdivision and Lewiston Industrial Track) was excluded from the graph so the route could not borrow a rival company's alignment.

properties.speed_source: estimated: a 5.4-mile branch worked as a connection off the main line; unsourced

segments.note: Passed to Canadian National with the rest of the Grand Trunk in 1923. A daily Montreal-Portland/Lewiston train was still running as of a 1954 timetable, the Lewiston portion working over this branch. Drawn to 1967 to match the end of Montreal service on the main line; note that the milepost source says the Lewiston station did not close until 1971, so service over the branch may have outlasted the through train by up to four years. Nobody has found a timetable settling that, so 1967 is a lower bound, not a documented last train. Frequency estimated/unsourced
sources: Segment-level (route and length only): the branch, its 1874 opening and its 5.4-mile length come from the milepost list for Lewiston Junction MP 29.7. The end year is NOT sourced at segment level -- see the note.
